title: The projective variety of Borel subgroups for a connected affine group
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field]. All algebraic groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Solvable groups, unipotent groups and tori have the meanings of [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]: solvability is termination of successive commutator subgroup schemes, a smooth group is unipotent when its geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation, and a torus is isomorphic to $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some $r\geq0$. A Borel subgroup of a smooth connected group is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup; a maximal torus is a torus subgroup maximal under inclusion. Let $G$ be smooth and connected. There is a nonempty smooth connected projective finite-type $k$-scheme $X=\mathcal B(G)$, in particular proper and separated over $k$ [def-pc-scheme, def-kun-projective, def-weil-proper-morphism], with an action $a:G\times_kX\to X$ satisfying the unit and multiplication identities, and a bijection $B\mapsto b_B$ from the Borel subgroups of $G$ to $X(k)$. This bijection identifies $g\cdot b_B$ with $b_{gBg^{-1}}$ for $g\in G(k)$, and $G(k)$ acts transitively on $X(k)$. For every Borel $B$, its point has scheme-theoretic stabilizer exactly $B$: for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, $$\{g\in G(A):g\cdot(b_B)_A=(b_B)_A\}=B(A).$$ Every torus subgroup of $G$ is contained in a Borel subgroup. For a torus $T\subseteq G$, the points fixed scheme-theoretically by $T$ are exactly the $b_B$ for which $T\subseteq B$. Here a point is fixed scheme-theoretically when the action identity holds after every commutative $k$-algebra extension.

proof.text: Choose a smooth connected solvable closed subgroup $B_0\subseteq G$ of greatest dimension; the identity subgroup makes this collection nonempty. The dimension assertions of [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] bound the possible dimensions by $\dim G$ and make a strict inclusion of smooth connected subgroups increase dimension. Hence $B_0$ is maximal and is a Borel subgroup. Solvability by termination of the derived series agrees with solvability by a finite normal series with commutative quotients: a terminating derived series is a normal series with commutative successive quotients, and for any normal series with commutative quotients induction puts the $i$th derived subgroup inside the $i$th member. No normality of $B_0$ in $G$ is needed for the dimension assertion.

source.place: Theorem 17.9, first sentence of proof, printed p.354; greatest-dimension choice explained before Example 17.7.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-subgroup-flag-realization] to $B_0$. Obtain a faithful representation on $V$ and a complete flag $\mathcal F$ with full scheme stabilizer $B_0$ in the projective finite-type scheme $Y=\operatorname{Fl}(V)$. The representation acts on the flag functor by sending each locally direct-summand submodule to its image; this defines its scheme action, with identities inherited from matrix multiplication. For any $\mathcal E\in Y(k)$ its stabilizer $K$ has a smooth connected solvable subgroup $K_{\mathrm{red}}^\circ$ of dimension $\dim K$. Maximality of the dimension of $B_0$ implies $\dim K\leq\dim B_0$. Thus [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] makes $O=G\mathcal F$ an orbit of minimum dimension $\dim G-\dim B_0$. If its boundary in its closure were nonempty, it would contain a $k$-point: [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] supplies a closed point of $Y$ in this nonempty closed subset, and [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base] identifies its residue field with $k$. The orbit node would give an orbit there of strictly smaller dimension, contradicting the minimum. Consequently $O$ is closed in $Y$.

source.place: Theorem 17.9, first paragraph of proof, printed p.354; orbit-boundary argument of Corollary 1.66; closed points: Stacks 0478 and 00FV/01TB.

proof.text: Put $X=O$ with its reduced scheme structure. The orbit node [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] gives smoothness and a faithfully flat, hence surjective, orbit map $q:G\to X$. The flag-realization node gives properness and finite type of this closed reduced subscheme. It is nonempty since it contains $\mathcal F$, and connected since a nontrivial clopen partition would pull back along the continuous surjection $q$ to a nontrivial clopen partition of $G$. Projectivity of $Y$ means it has a closed embedding into some $\mathbf P^N_k$ [def-kun-projective]; composing $X\hookrightarrow Y$ with that embedding is a closed immersion by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-comp], so $X$ is projective in the required convention. The invariant-closure assertion of the orbit node shows that the flag action $G\times_kY\to Y$ maps the closed subscheme $G\times_kX$ set-theoretically into $X$. Since $G\times_kX\to X$ is the base change of the smooth $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $X$ is reduced, $G\times_kX$ is reduced by [lem-sfb-smooth-algebra-over-reduced-ring], applied on affine charts. A morphism from a reduced scheme whose image lies in a closed subset factors uniquely through its reduced closed subscheme, so the action restricts to $G\times_kX\to X$; its action identities are the restrictions of those on $Y$, by the same uniqueness. Finally [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry], applied to $\mathcal F$, identifies $q$ with $G\to G/B_0$ and gives separatedness and $X(k)=G(k)/B_0(k)$.

source.place: Theorem 17.9, first paragraph, printed p.354; Section 17f, printed p.368; Proposition 7.30, printed pp.146--147. Closed-immersion composition: Stacks 01QS (lemma-composition-closed-immersion).

proof.text: Let $B$ be any Borel subgroup. Its restricted action on nonempty proper $X$ satisfies the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-solvable-proper-fixed-point], so there is $x\in X(k)$ fixed scheme-theoretically by $B$. Write $x=g\mathcal F$ with $g\in G(k)$, using the rational-point lifting clause of [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]. For every $k$-algebra $A$, the equality $h g\mathcal F_A=g\mathcal F_A$ is equivalent to $g^{-1}hg\in B_0(A)$, since the scheme stabilizer of $\mathcal F$ is $B_0$. Hence $B\subseteq gB_0g^{-1}$ as subgroup schemes. The latter is smooth connected solvable, so maximality of $B$ forces $B=gB_0g^{-1}$. This proves conjugacy without assuming reductivity.

source.place: Theorem 17.9, last paragraph of proof, printed p.354.

proof.text: For $B=gB_0g^{-1}$ define $b_B=g\mathcal F\in X(k)$. If also $B=g'B_0g'^{-1}$, then $g^{-1}g'$ normalizes $B_0$. By [lem-sfb-borel-scheme-normalizer] it belongs to $B_0(k)$, so $g\mathcal F=g'\mathcal F$. Conversely that equality puts $g^{-1}g'$ in $B_0(k)$ and implies equality of the conjugate subgroups. Thus the assignment is well-defined and injective. It is surjective since every point of $X(k)$ is $g\mathcal F$ by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]. For $h\in G(k)$, $h b_B=hg\mathcal F=b_{hBh^{-1}}$. Moreover $g' g^{-1}$ sends $g\mathcal F$ to $g'\mathcal F$, giving transitivity. Calling this scheme with its labels $\mathcal B(G)$ produces the requested variety of Borels.

source.place: Section 17f, printed pp.368--369; Theorem 17.48, printed p.367 (the Section 17f reference to 17.47 is a numbering slip).

proof.text:
For any $k$-algebra $A$ and $u\in G(A)$, with $B=gB_0g^{-1}$ as above, compute
$$u(b_B)_A=(b_B)_A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (g^{-1}ug)\mathcal F_A=\mathcal F_A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g^{-1}ug\in B_0(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in B(A).$$
The middle equivalence uses the full scheme-theoretic flag stabilizer from [lem-sfb-solvable-subgroup-flag-realization], not just its rational points. This proves the stabilizer assertion even for nonreduced $A$.

source.place: Section 17f, printed p.368, with the all-algebras stabilizer interpretation of Theorem 4.27 and Proposition 7.29.

proof.text: Let $T\subseteq G$ be any torus, including the rank-zero torus. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, $T\simeq(\mathbf G_m)^r=\operatorname{Spec}k[\mathbf Z^r]$. By [lem-trf-split-lattice-torus-projection] this scheme is smooth and its coordinate algebra is a domain. Its zero prime is a generic point, so its spectrum is nonempty and irreducible, hence connected. Its group law is commutative, so it is solvable. Choose a smooth connected solvable subgroup containing $T$ with greatest dimension. As in step 1, the strict dimension increase in [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] makes it maximal among all smooth connected solvable subgroups: any larger subgroup would still contain $T$. This is a Borel containing $T$.

source.place: Theorem 17.10, proof, and paragraph following Definition 17.12, printed p.355; split torus coordinates as in Section 12a.

proof.text: Every $x\in X(k)$ is a unique $b_B$. The stabilizer calculation in step 6 shows that $T$ fixes $b_B$ after every commutative $k$-algebra extension if and only if $T(A)\subseteq B(A)$ for every such algebra $A$. These inclusions are exactly factorization of the subgroup morphism $T\hookrightarrow G$ through the closed subgroup $B$ (apply them to the universal point of affine $T$, or equivalently Yoneda). Thus the fixed rational points are precisely the $b_B$ with $T\subseteq B$, in the stipulated scheme-theoretic sense.

source.place: Lemma 17.52 and the example following it, printed p.369; all-algebras form follows from the previously proved stabilizer formula.
